subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Direct Trade vs. Fair Trade
description: Learn Direct Trade vs. Fair Trade in one minute.

hook.text: Direct Trade skips certifications. Roasters visit farms, negotiate prices, and build long-term relationships.

buildup.text: Direct Trade often pays farmers 25–100% above Fair Trade prices by eliminating intermediary costs.

discovery.text: Without third-party auditing, Direct Trade relies on the roaster's integrity. There's no independent verification.

twist.text: Some roasters use 'Direct Trade' as marketing without actually visiting farms or paying premium prices.

climax.text: Both models try to fix the same problem—farmer poverty—but through different mechanisms with different flaws.

punchline.text: Labels promise fairness. The details determine if it's real.

quiz.question: What is the main criticism of Direct Trade?
options: There's no independent verification of claims

details.summary: Direct trade bypasses traditional middlemen by connecting roasters directly with farmers. Unlike fair trade, it has no third-party certification. Roasters negotiate prices individually, typically paying well above fair trade minimums.
details.whyItMatters: Direct trade represents the specialty coffee industry's attempt to pay farmers more while getting better quality. It shows that relationship-based trade can supplement certifications.
takeaways: Direct trade has no standardized certification body
Prices paid typically exceed fair trade minimums
It relies on relationship and trust rather than third-party audit

faq.question: Is direct trade better than fair trade for farmers?
faq.answer: Direct trade often pays higher prices for higher quality, but it reaches far fewer farmers. Fair trade provides a safety net for millions. The two approaches serve different needs: direct trade rewards excellence while fair trade provides baseline protection.

faq.question: How can consumers verify direct trade claims?
faq.answer: Without certification, verification relies on the roaster's transparency. Look for named farms, published prices paid, and evidence of ongoing relationships. Some roasters publish full supply chain information. Skepticism is healthy when claims cannot be independently verified.
